modules.doc:
The reading index: recognised notes parsed once and queried by scope, order and
filter, with every read bounded and cancellable.

This replaces the one-day-at-a-time reader. A day is not a note, an address is
not unique across destinations, and a thought's recorded day may differ from
its note's filename — so the reference needs every recognised note, parsed
lazily and invalidated per path, rather than a fresh whole-vault parse on every
keystroke.

The index is never write authority. It reads, caches and orders; a write is
revalidated against the note itself by the writer. The one rule it must not
break is honesty about gaps: a file it could not read is reported, never
counted as an empty scope, and a query that a newer generation superseded is
discarded rather than installed.

Pure of every Obsidian API: paths, text and a generation are injected.

exports.name: ThoughtIndexPorts
exports.doc: How the index reads the vault.

exports.name: ThoughtIndex
exports.doc:
The lazy, invalidatable reading index.

A query reads only the notes it needs, deduplicating concurrent reads of the
same path and keeping at most four in flight; a modify/create/delete/rename
invalidates exactly the affected path so the next query re-reads it.

modules.doc:
The one writer of a day note.

A note has exactly one writer at a time: an active editing buffer, or
`Vault.process` otherwise — never both. Reading view's dormant buffer is not a
writer. Two writers is what made
Obsidian report the file as modified externally: the day-stats pass landed on
disk behind an editor holding the same note, and the editor's next keystroke
wrote over it (or lost the race the other way round).

The second rule is that a plan is built from the text being written. The
rewrite callback is handed the exact string that will be replaced, inside the
writer, so an append cannot land on a document that moved since it was read.

exports.name: dispatchDraftChange
exports.signature: export function dispatchDraftChange(view: EditorView, transaction: TransactionSpec): void
exports.doc:
Dispatches a change to the composer's owned, fileless editor buffer.

This is not a note write: it accepts no file or vault, and preserves the
caller's input/history annotations. Publishing a draft still uses a capture
plan through the ordinary note writer.

exports.name: RewriteResult
exports.doc: One write: its changes, the resulting text, and where the caret belongs.

exports.name: Rewrite
exports.signature: export type Rewrite = (source: string) => RewriteResult | null
exports.doc: Builds a rewrite against the text it is given; `null` means "nothing to do".

exports.name: RewriteRefused
exports.doc:
A rewrite that was refused before the document was touched.

The distinction matters to a capture: a refusal means the note is exactly as
it was, so the writer may submit again, while a failure after the dispatch
means the answer is unknown and nothing may be written twice.

exports.doc: Hooks that let a caller observe — or veto — one write before it happens.

Confirms an already-written submission without writing it again.

When the live editor holds the expected bytes but the file does not, the
editor is the truth and the recovery is to let it save — then read the file.
It never dispatches an old plan and never replaces newer text: if no editor
holds exactly `expected`, it does nothing and reports false.

Registers one in-flight Loom write so a Check or Retry can await it.

A check that read the note while an old attempt could still commit would draw
the wrong conclusion; registering before the write and removing in `finally`
is the IO-lifetime guard, not stored product state. Returns a release function.

modules.doc:
Weaver: a day note is a linear list of entries, and a thought may be written
from anywhere.

An entry is `{ B.D.N }`, its prose, and one clock row `[+-=] HH:MM:SS YYYY-MM-DD
HH:MM:SS`. Writing happens in two places that share one writer: inside a note,
where the entry is the note's own text, and in the floating composer, which
holds one unsaved thought until it is settled. The navigator is the only list
and the only navigation.

This module is wiring, and only wiring: settings, the one writer, the one clock,
the composer, the invitation dock, the workspace service, commands, and the two
listeners that keep derived facts (day counters, portal association) true.

exports.name: WeaverPlugin
exports.signature: export default class WeaverPlugin extends Plugin
exports.doc: Wiring only: settings, editor extensions, commands, and the two derived facts.

modules.doc:
The model a whisper comes from.

One interface, two implementations: `NoModel` — the default, and what every
test runs — and `OmLxModel`, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

The call goes through `obsidian`'s `requestUrl`, not `fetch`: it is not subject
to the renderer's CORS rules, it needs no `cors_origins` setting on the server,
and a mobile webview cannot block it. It also means an unreachable endpoint
resolves as a failed response rather than a thrown network error, which is the
shape this module already handles.

exports.name: WhisperRequest
exports.doc: One completion request, already assembled.

exports.name: WhisperFailure
exports.doc:
Why a completion produced no text.

The distinction is not cosmetic: an endpoint that refused this device and an
endpoint that never answered are the same silence to the idle speculation, and
completely different sentences to a writer who pressed a command.

exports.name: WhisperReply
exports.doc: What a completion produced: the model's text, or the reason there is none.

exports.name: WhisperModel
exports.doc: The model a whisper comes from. `id` is the name the endpoint is asked for.

exports.name: NoModel
exports.doc:
Nothing is generated and nothing is written: the default, and what `npm test`
uses.

It answers `unreachable` rather than throwing, because every caller already
treats "no whisper" as ordinary; the runner never asks it anything at all,
since it is the id that turns the whole feature off.

exports.name: OmLxModel
exports.doc:
oMLX's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, one non-streaming completion per call.

`reasoning_content` is never read: a reply that carries reasoning and no
content is empty content, which is this class's whole handling of thinking
models. `max_tokens: 320` is a decision, not a default — three rows of up to
fourteen words plus the JSON envelope need roughly 150 tokens, and the cap is
what stops a model from rambling into a minute-long answer.

modules.doc:
The runner: when a whisper is asked for, and what becomes of the answer.

Two entry points, because the writer's two paths through an entry are
different. `arm` is speculation during a pause in typing: it (re)starts a
short timer, and an answer that arrives before the writer presses `⏎` is
cached, so settle can write it inside its own transaction. `request` is settle
finding the cache cold: it asks at once and lands the answer through the
engine, as its own undoable transaction. Nothing waits on a model.

Failures are counted, not reported. Two transport failures in a row and this
device stops asking until it reloads — a laptop that has left the machine
running oMLX behind should not spend a request per keystroke finding that out.
A *validation* failure does not count: the endpoint answered, the writer's
register was not met.

Reading view: the close mark, muted and labelled.

A `✓` line is a decision, not an entry, so it is styled in place and never
wrapped in a frame.

exports.name: createCloseProcessor

Styles the rendered closing mark.

Only a class and a label are added: the text is the record, and rewriting it

modules.doc:
Reading view: the same entry the editor draws, in the same frame.

The address paragraph becomes the frame's first child and the clock paragraph
its last; the prose between them is the frame's interior. The wrapper is a real
element because a box needs one to enclose — and because the file's own text is
what labels it: the address row is the top rail's label, and the clock row is the
bottom edge, its duration at the left corner and its moment at the right. The
rails run through the middle of those rows and are cut behind them by the
labels' own backgrounds, so the box reads as running into its own text.

The address's own characters are kept, split into digit runs so the digits stay
white and the punctuation takes the dimension's colour. Anything typed after
the address stays in the DOM untouched, links and emphasis included. A persistent
top-right link labels a recorded creation day only when it differs from the
day-note filename. Awaiting and historical undated entries carry no date link.
The label never reads the wall clock, and the clock row's two halves stay
time-only: digit and punctuation runs, exactly as in the editor.

The tab owns no rules of its own — it writes the settings model and calls
`commit()`, so the effect of a control is always `settings.ts` plus `css.ts`.

Realms are the one group that edits a list, so it is the one group that
has to be careful with stored data: a row it does not understand is shown with
its reason and left in place, and nothing is rewritten into a shape the writer
did not ask for.

Settings UI, in five groups: what is written, where the day note is, how an
entry looks, what reads it, and the rest.

Every control writes through `commit()` so changes apply live.

modules.doc:
Weaver settings model.

This module is deliberately free of any `obsidian` import so the
normalization rules can be unit-tested in plain Node. The settings tab lives
in `settings-tab.ts`.

A field's name is the product's word for the thing: `entrySize`, never
`headingSize`. `heading` is Markdown syntax here, and a setting that draws an
entry is not about syntax. The v2 spellings survive in exactly one place —
`LEGACY_SETTING_KEYS` — because a vault's saved `data.json` is data, not code,
and renaming a field must not silently reset it.

exports.name: WeaverSettings
exports.doc: Every setting Weaver has, in the groups the tab shows them in.

exports.name: WeaverData
exports.doc: What is on disk: a version, one settings object, and the shared Reviews.

exports.signature: export function whisperReachable(endpoint: string, mobile: boolean): boolean
exports.doc:
True when this device can reach a whisper endpoint at all.

`data.json` syncs, so a loopback endpoint travels with the vault and means *the
reader's own device*. On a phone that is guaranteed to reach nothing, so the
phone does not ask: capture is untouched, rendering is complete, and the
address the writer sets is one both machines can reach.

Normalizes any persisted payload into a complete, clamped settings object.
Unknown fields are dropped; invalid values fall back to the defaults; a v2
field name keeps its value under the v3 name.

exports.doc:
Normalizes persisted plugin data. A bare settings object written by an earlier
build is wrapped instead of being discarded, and every payload is reported as
the current version — the migration is the normalization. Shared Reviews are
decoded leniently here; a store that must refuse to overwrite unreadable data
checks the raw envelope itself.

emphasis colours, and the six anchor colours. Nothing is generated per level —
depth rides on the `--weaver-d` custom property a line carries, so a deeper
entry costs nothing.

The anchor colours are emitted as custom properties for the portal's
multicolour rail, which is the only surface that needs the palette as a
whole. It reads `--weaver-anchor-1` … `--weaver-anchor-6` rather than
restating the hex values in the stylesheet: one palette, one place to change
it.

exports.name: applyCss
exports.doc:
Writes the stylesheet into a single `<style>` element in `<head>`. Reusing one
element keeps the DOM stable across settings changes.

exports.name: removeCss
exports.doc: Removes the injected stylesheet on unload.

modules.doc:
The entry-day link at the top right of a frame: `[[YYYY.MM.DD]]`.

The entry's clock row records its day when one was written; a historical
undated row inherits the day-note filename, and the label is written in that
filename's own dotted or dashed style. This generated label names that
recorded day, never the date of viewing. The `weaver-frame-label` background
cuts the top rail behind it. Both surfaces build the same element here, so
Live Preview and Reading view agree.

The element is a span with `role="link"`, not an anchor: the surfaces own the
navigation — `openLinkText` — and an anchor would let Obsidian's own handler
fire a second navigation on top of it.

exports.name: OpenDayLink
exports.signature: export type OpenDayLink = (target: string, sourcePath: string) => void
exports.doc: Open a day note by its basename, relative to the note on screen.

exports.name: dayLinkElement
exports.signature: export function dayLinkElement( target: string, sourcePath: string, open: OpenDayLink ): HTMLElement
exports.doc:
The link element for `target` (`2026.11.02`), opened from `sourcePath`.

A click or Enter/Space activates it; the event is stopped so the editor does
not also move the caret into the widget. `open` is called with the target and
the note it was clicked from, exactly as `workspace.openLinkText` wants them.

modules.doc:
The digit-and-ink grammar: `B.D.N`, the clock row and the date label all split
the same way — digits in the note's own text colour, punctuation in the
dimension's.

Shared by the navigator, the Live Preview frames and the Reading-view frame —
one grammar, every surface. The address's hyphen is punctuation like every other
separator, because on a framed surface the whole address is the top rail's label
and its background cuts the rail; there is no character that belongs to the box
instead of the text.

exports.name: NUM_CLASS
exports.doc: The class digits carry: the note's own text colour.

exports.name: INK_CLASS
exports.doc: The class punctuation carries: the dimension's colour.

exports.name: Slice
exports.doc: A piece of `B.D.N`: its text, and the class it carries.

exports.name: addressSlices
exports.doc:
The runs an address is drawn in: digits white, punctuation coloured. Pure, so the
editor's decoration set and the Reading view build the same runs from the same
rule.

exports.name: appendDigitRuns
exports.signature: export function appendDigitRuns(parent: HTMLElement, text: string): void
exports.doc: Splits `B.D.N` into digit runs and separators inside `parent`.

exports.name: appendClockRuns
exports.signature: export function appendClockRuns(parent: HTMLElement, clock: string): HTMLElement[]
exports.doc:
Splits an `HH:MM:SS` clock into digit runs and separator runs inside `parent`:
each colon is `.weaver-duration-ink` (the dimension's colour), each digit run
`.weaver-duration-num` (the note's own text colour). Returns the digit spans in
order, so a ticking clock can write into them.

modules.doc:
How an invitation is named, in the words a writer reads.

Kept out of the dock so the same strings serve the navigator, the notice and
the accessible labels: one invitation, one wording. Every label here is a
function of a frozen occurrence and the current instant, so a countdown can be
repainted without touching any other state.

exports.name: InvitationView
exports.doc: One invitation as a surface shows it: the occurrence, and how near it is.

exports.name: openingTime
exports.doc: The opening's own local hour and minute, `09:11`.

exports.name: countdownLabel
exports.signature: export function countdownLabel(occurrence: PortalOccurrence, now: number): string
exports.doc:
`Opens in 09:30`, rounded up so a countdown never reads `00:00` before its
opening, or the empty string once it is open.

exports.name: arrivalLabel
exports.signature: export function arrivalLabel(occurrence: PortalOccurrence, contextName?: string): string
exports.doc: `09:11 · Spanish`: when it opens, and the destination it invites writing into.

exports.name: invitationName
exports.doc: The schedule's own name, or a sentence when it has none.

modules.doc:
The loom's timing group: one beginning clock and one writing duration, in the
shared digit grammar — icon, white digits, dimension-coloured colons.

An unknown value draws a single `—` over digit runs that stay in the DOM, so a
known value returns without rebuilding nodes. `update` paints one explicit
reading and reports whether the drawn duration changed; no timer, no clock.

exports.name: LoomTimingMode
exports.doc: What a timing group is showing.

exports.name: LoomTimingReading
exports.doc: One explicit reading; the caller samples every field and supplies no clock.

exports.name: LoomTiming
exports.doc:
One timing group inside `parent`: beginning first, writing duration second.
Built once by the constructor; mounted wherever the timing belongs.

modules.doc:
The Loom: the one compact surface a thought is written in, from anywhere.

It is a single non-modal dialog with a small header and persistent Markdown
writing pane. Desktop retains an identity line and footer actions; mobile
places circular actions beside the content-sized prose, with duration below.
The destination control opens a chooser in place
of the prose, so the writer never scrolls past destination machinery to reach
the words. Reference context is optional and starts collapsed; it is a second
persistent pane, read-only, with its own navigation. A saved thought keeps the
same editor node, its history and its scroll, and turns read-only instead of
being replaced by rendered HTML.

The renderer owns only presentation and ephemeral interaction: mounted DOM,
the composing flag, measurements and a hint overlay. Every semantic action is
a command on the controller or the reference owner, so the note is never
written by opening, browsing, hiding or resizing this surface.

exports.name: CaptureSurface
exports.doc: The lower surface the Loom reads and commands; either controller satisfies it.

exports.name: LoomHost
exports.doc: What the Loom needs from the plugin.

exports.name: LoomInvitation
exports.doc: An opening offered by the scheduler: upcoming, or in its available minute.

exports.name: Loom
exports.doc: The one compact Loom surface.

modules.doc:
A persistent, fileless Obsidian Markdown editor and read-only native rendering.

The native editor owns formatting, history, suggestions and toolbar commands.
Its MarkdownView never receives a file: autosave has no note to write, and
publishing remains the capture controller's decision. A bound editor context
registers the focused draft with Obsidian without activating another leaf.
Read-only rendering retains the editor, its source, history and selection.

exports.name: PaneSelection
exports.doc: A caret or selected range in the pane's Markdown source.

exports.name: MarkdownPaneOptions
exports.doc: Mounting dependencies and callbacks for a persistent Markdown pane.

exports.name: MarkdownPane
exports.doc: A native fileless editor whose lifetime survives saving and hiding.

modules.doc:
Which platform this is, as one answer.

Every surface asks here rather than reading Obsidian's flags itself, so a phone
is a phone in the CSS, in the keys and in the pinning alike.

exports.name: isPhone
exports.doc:
Phone detection with the documented fallback: older runtimes may not expose
`Platform.isPhone`, in which case Obsidian's own body class is authoritative.

exports.name: isMobile
exports.doc: True on a phone or a tablet, from Obsidian's own flags.

exports.name: isTablet
exports.doc: True on a tablet, which is neither a phone nor a desktop window.

exports.name: canHover
exports.doc: True when the pointer can hover, so tooltips and hover states are useful.
